section_summary: This section follows U.S., British and Japanese discussions about rebuilding Japan’s cotton textile and rayon industries without imposing permanent limits on peaceful production or exports. It includes industry meetings, production statistics, correspondence about rayon and synthetic fibers, and reports on Japanese textile markets and prices. The final documents address a proposed British-American industry mission to Japan and clarify that its visitors would have no official status.

subfiles.title: Proposals to Limit Japanese Cotton Textile Spindleage
subfiles.about: Interdepartmental participants considered a British proposal to cap Japanese cotton spindleage.
subfiles.summary: Officials agreed that limiting Japanese spindles to 3.5 million would hinder economic recovery and conflict with U.S. trade policy. They also opposed encouraging a governmental body to consider production limits.

subfiles.title: Airgram on Proposed Textile Mission and British Proposals
subfiles.about: Tokyo reported on British proposals concerning Japanese textiles; much of the OCR is illegible.
subfiles.summary: The airgram appears to discuss a proposed British-American textile mission, Japanese textile policy, most-favored-nation treatment and the Havana Charter. Its wording cannot be reliably recovered from the supplied OCR.

subfiles.title: Reply on British-American Textile Mission
subfiles.about: State reported discussions with British and American textile representatives and set limits for any mission.
subfiles.summary: State described British and U.S. industry requests for a mission to Japan. It maintained that Japanese textiles should compete without permanent production limits and that any mission must remain within an information giving and fact finding role, with no authority to fix prices, divide markets or limit output.

subfiles.title: British Request for a Joint Textile Industry Mission
subfiles.about: British officials requested an invitation for a joint industry mission to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Minister Taylor sought a mission to discuss Japan’s long term textile role. U.S. officials raised objections to private restrictions on Japanese exports and warned that official sponsorship could appear to sanction limits on peaceful industries.

subfiles.title: Note on Timing of SCAP Instructions
subfiles.about: A note says instructions to SCAP would await the February 3 meeting with U.S. textile representatives.
subfiles.summary: Instructions to SCAP were deferred pending the industry meeting.

subfiles.title: Japanese Textile Competition and Sterling Area Currency Restrictions
subfiles.about: U.S. textile representatives discussed Japanese competition and barriers to exports into the sterling area.
subfiles.summary: Industry representatives raised falling export prices, future Japanese competition and sterling area dollar restrictions. Martin reaffirmed U.S. opposition to limits on peaceful Japanese industries and invited a detailed written mission proposal. Officials said any mission should exchange information, while specific evidence of currency discrimination could be examined.

subfiles.title: United States and United Kingdom Textile Mission to Japan
subfiles.about: Sir Raymond Streat urged an early decision on a joint textile industry mission.
subfiles.summary: Streat described the mission as a review of world cotton trade with SCAP and Japanese industry, without explicitly seeking an export agreement. Martin said U.S. industry had not yet requested approval; Streat favored an early announcement and an autumn visit.

subfiles.title: Airgram on Japanese Textile Industry
subfiles.about: An incoming airgram concerns Japanese textiles, but its substantive text is unreadable in the supplied OCR.
subfiles.summary: The March 5 airgram’s substantive text cannot be reliably identified.

subfiles.title: Japanese Rayon Industry
subfiles.about: A memorandum and tables review Japanese rayon production, projected recovery and historic export markets.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum summarizes Army projections of 250 million pounds of Japanese rayon production and 82.5 million pounds of exports by 1953, both below 1938 peaks. It considers raw materials and possible renewed competition with U.S. producers. Attached tables give world and Japanese production, capacity projections, and historic exports of rayon fabrics, yarn and staple fiber by destination.

subfiles.title: Development of Japanese Rayon Industry
subfiles.about: Rayon industry representatives discussed Japan’s capacity, exports, raw materials and patents with U.S. officials.
subfiles.summary: Rose sought clarification of U.S. policy and warned against rebuilding excess Japanese rayon capacity. Officials discussed pulp supplies, inefficient plants, export markets and the need for Japan to become self supporting. Rose also raised Austrian rayon rehabilitation and Japanese patent access.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Rayon Industry Conversation Memorandum
subfiles.to: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The March 15 rayon conversation memorandum was sent to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Encloses the March 15 memorandum for the Acting Political Adviser.

subfiles.title: Development of Japanese Rayon Industry, Enclosed Copy
subfiles.to: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: An enclosed copy records the March 15 discussion of Japan’s rayon industry.
subfiles.summary: This is a duplicate of the memorandum on pages 174–176. It covers proposed rayon expansion, pulp and coal constraints, plant efficiency, export markets, Austrian rayon and patent questions.

subfiles.title: Reply to H. Wickliffe Rose on Japanese Patents
subfiles.about: Martin answered Rose’s questions about filing and accessing patents connected with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Martin said restrictions on patent applications in Japan had been removed for Japanese and foreign applicants. He explained licensing policy for vested Japanese patents in the United States and enclosed two policy releases.

subfiles.title: Rayon Industry Book Sent to State Department
subfiles.about: O'Brien arranged to send Rose’s book on Japan’s rayon and synthetic fiber industry.
subfiles.summary: Offers a separately mailed copy of Rose’s book.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Rayon Industry Book
subfiles.about: Cale acknowledged O'Brien’s letter about sending Rose’s book.
subfiles.summary: Thanks O'Brien for arranging to send the book.

subfiles.title: Airgram on Japanese Textile Mill Production
subfiles.about: Tokyo forwarded textile production information; most numerical detail is obscured by OCR.
subfiles.summary: The airgram appears to relay Textile Division figures on Japanese mill or printing production, but the supplied OCR is too damaged for reliable quantities.

subfiles.title: Recent Developments in the Japanese Textile Industry
subfiles.about: SCAP Textile Division chief Cleaves reviewed cotton, gloves, silk and rayon in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Cleaves reported weak cotton textile orders, unused spindleage and limited stocks, while explaining Japanese costs and sterling area prospects. He disputed U.S. woolen glove industry complaints, described accumulating silk stocks and questioned complaints from Paterson weavers. He also reported that India’s halted imports and inefficient production were hurting Japanese rayon.

subfiles.title: Japanese Inability to Meet Indonesian Textile Needs
subfiles.about: Shohan summarized SCAP’s response on Japan’s ability to fill an Indonesian textile order.
subfiles.summary: Only 65 million yards could be supplied quickly from port stocks; new production would take substantially longer.

subfiles.title: Japanese Textile Availabilities for Indonesia
subfiles.about: Shohan assessed inventories and production against a proposed Dutch purchase for Indonesia.
subfiles.summary: Estimates Japanese production and stocks; notes Army’s inquiry to SCAP about meeting a 120–130 million yard order.

subfiles.title: Telegram on Financing Japanese Textiles for Indonesia
subfiles.about: The message outlines proposed ECA financing, import permits and bank credits for Indonesian textile purchases.
subfiles.summary: The legible portions describe a sequence involving Indonesian import permits, contracts with Japanese suppliers, letters of credit, shipping documents and yen payments. Tokyo urges prompt arrangements so deliveries can meet the proposed schedule; portions of the first page are unreadable.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Publications on Polyvinyl Synthetic Fiber
subfiles.from: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Tokyo transmitted two Kurashiki Rayon publications on vinylon and its textile products.
subfiles.summary: The despatch summarizes Dr. Tomonari’s claim that vinylon could be produced from domestic Japanese materials and aid recovery. It describes Kurashiki Rayon’s plants and encloses publications on polyvinyl fiber development and a Tokyo vinylon exhibition.

subfiles.title: British-American Cotton Textile Industry Conference
subfiles.about: American industry representatives sought U.S. views on a proposed joint visit to Japanese textile interests.
subfiles.summary: Industry representatives described a proposed survey mission to Japan and said they would avoid agreements restricting Japanese trade. State officials stressed that any visit would have no governmental authority to negotiate limits and would be confined to fact finding. The officials agreed to review the group’s public statement and seek SCAP’s views.

subfiles.title: Abolition of Floor Prices by Japan
subfiles.about: A Netherlands Embassy representative questioned Japan’s removal of minimum export prices.
subfiles.summary: Jobsis feared cheap Japanese textile exports and possible dumping. U.S. officials described higher wages, misleading price comparisons and continued post audit scrutiny of export prices, while linking trade recovery to Japan’s stability.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Floor Price Memorandum to Tokyo
subfiles.to: Acting U.S. Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Doherty forwarded the December 7 floor price memorandum for SCAP’s information.
subfiles.summary: Attaches the December 7 memorandum for SCAP.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Floor Price Memorandum to The Hague
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge, American Mission, The Hague
subfiles.about: Doherty forwarded the December 7 floor price memorandum to The Hague.
subfiles.summary: Attaches the December 7 memorandum for the American Mission.

subfiles.title: Army Copy of Airgram A-248 on Proposed Textile Mission
subfiles.about: State relayed Army objections to a British-American textile survey mission.
subfiles.summary: The message repeats Under Secretary West’s view that the mission would divert SCAP’s time amid trade procedure changes and efforts to expand Japanese exports. It adds that the earlier State message’s Army clearance problem was a misunderstanding.

subfiles.title: Army Telegram WAR 97613 on Proposed Textile Mission
subfiles.from: Robert R. West, Office of the Under Secretary of the Army
subfiles.about: West advised SCAP that the proposed textile mission was inappropriate at that time.
subfiles.summary: West argued that the mission would consume SCAP time without serving occupation needs.

subfiles.title: State Airgram A-248 on Proposed Textile Mission
subfiles.about: State supplied Tokyo with West’s Army telegram and explained the clearance misunderstanding.
subfiles.summary: This is the State airgram copied in the Army message on pages 204–205. It repeats West’s objections to the proposed mission and explains that State had cleared its earlier telegram with Friele.

subfiles.title: Textile Mission to Japan
subfiles.about: The British Embassy accepted SCAP’s terms for unofficial industry visitors and asked about joint consultation.
subfiles.summary: Burns accepted that visitors would have no official status; Schaetzel saw no objection to joint consultation.
